source.title_on_document: Homogenizing effect of large language models (LLMs) on creative diversity: An empirical comparison of human and ChatGPT writing

paper_design_summary: Three preregistered studies compare college admissions essays written by real applicants to a private East Coast university (2018-2022, before ChatGPT) with essays generated by GPT-4 from the same prompt, 2,200 essays in total. No person received AI help: GPT-4 conditions vary the model version, prompting (naive 'be as creative as possible', chain-of-thought with generated personal backgrounds) and parameters (presence and frequency penalty). Each essay is scored for individual diversity (Divergent Semantic Integration, BERT word embeddings), and each authorship group for a diversity growth rate (slope of collective semantic diversity on the log number of essays pooled).

studies.label: Study 1: 100 human vs 100 base GPT-4 admissions essays

assignment.what_was_assigned: No person was assigned to anything. 100 human essays were randomly sampled from an archive of applicant essays and compared with 100 essays that the authors generated with GPT-4 through the ChatGPT chat interface.
assignment.quote: We compared a set of 100 essays written by humans randomly chosen from submissions between 2018 and 2022 with another set of 100 essays generated using GPT-4.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 2, Section 3.2 (OSF https://osf.io/ywap5/registrations; Study 1 registered July 5, 2023; deviations in Tables S9-S10)

arms.name: Human
arms.description: 100 archival admissions essays by applicants, 2018-2022, randomly sampled

arms.name: Base GPT-4
arms.description: 100 essays generated by GPT-4 via the ChatGPT chat interface (June 24-30, 2023), one new chat per essay, prompt 'As a college applicant, please generate my admissions essay of approximately 650 words...'

participants.exclusions: Essays used in pilot studies (about 1,000) were excluded from the archive pool of 49,804 essays; titles and footers were removed from GPT-4 essays.
participants.who: No participants. Human essays are archival essays submitted by college applicants to a private East Coast university, 2018-2022. The paper counts essays, not authors (200 essays in this study).
participants.quote: We randomly selected human-written essays used in Studies 1-3 from the archival data submitted by applicants to a private East Coast university from 2018 to 2022 before the public launch of ChatGPT.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 via the ChatGPT chat interface (June 24-30, 2023)
ai_tool.how_used: GPT-4 wrote the essays on its own from the admissions prompt; no human used it.

task.description: College admissions essay: 'As OOOO University is a diverse community, the Admissions Committee would like to know more about you in your words. Please submit a brief essay, either personal or creative, which you feel best describes you.' GPT-4 asked for about 650 words.

outcomes.name: Individual diversity (Divergent Semantic Integration, DSI) of each essay
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: DSI: average cosine distance between all word pairs in an essay, BERT bert-large-uncased embeddings from layers 6 and 7, multiplied by 1,000. Paper treats higher DSI as greater creativity. Robustness: Sentence-BERT all-mpnet-base-v2 (Figs. S1-S3, Tables S6-S7, not in this PDF).

contrasts.reported: Human 829.59 (SD 7.92, n = 100) vs Base GPT-4 820.64 (SD 4.64, n = 100); Human minus Base GPT-4 Mean Difference = 8.95, 95% CI [7.14, 10.76], t(159.89) = 9.75, p < .001, Cohen's d = 1.38 (Welch t-test)
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 4.2.1; p. 6, Fig. 1 and Table 1

outcomes.name: Diversity growth rate (DGR) of collective diversity
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Collective diversity = DSI of 34 sentences sampled from a pooled group of k essays (k = 2 to 34), averaged over 5,000 draws; DGR = slope b on ln(number of essays) by authorship group; doubling effect = b x ln(2). Main paper text: the human DGR minus base GPT-4 DGR.

contrasts.reported: DGR Human b = 0.58, 95% CI [0.50, 0.66], doubling effect 0.40, SE 0.04, df 62, t = 15.35; Base GPT-4 b = 0.18, 95% CI [0.11, 0.26], doubling 0.13, SE 0.04, df 62, t = 4.82. Human minus Base GPT-4 slope: b = 0.40, 95% CI [0.29, 0.50], p < .001; base GPT-4 about 31% of the human rate
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 4.2.2; p. 6, Table 2; p. 7, Fig. 2

diversity_detail.metric: Diversity growth rate: slope of collective semantic diversity (word-pair cosine distance over 34 sampled sentences) on ln(number of essays)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pooled groups of 2 to 34 essays within each authorship condition; all word pairs among 34 sampled sentences, 5,000 resamples per group size; 33 collective-diversity scores per condition
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Multiple regression of collective diversity on ln(number of essays), authorship dummies and interactions (33 points per condition, df 62); pairwise slope comparison
diversity_detail.notes: Not a similarity across people who used AI; compares the diversity of a human essay pool with a pool of GPT-4 outputs. n_units = 66 is 33 scores x 2 conditions, inferred from p. 4 and df in Table 2.

eligibility.reason: All three studies compare archival human-written admissions essays with essays generated by GPT-4 alone; no person was assigned to or received AI help, and there are no participants (counts are essays: 200, 400 and 1,600). Outcomes are computed on the essays (DSI and diversity growth rate), so the paper is AI-versus-human context evidence.

one_line_finding: Across 2,200 admissions essays, human essays had higher individual semantic diversity than base GPT-4 essays (Study 1 d = 1.38) and a higher diversity growth rate (Study 1 b = 0.58 vs 0.18; Study 3 0.62 vs 0.07), and the gap in growth rate persisted with naive prompts, raised penalties and chain-of-thought prompting (pp. 5-8, Tables 1-2).
open_questions: Table 1 (p. 6) prints the 95% CI for CoT-prompted minus Base GPT-4 in Study 3 as [-1.43, 3.33], which includes zero, while the same row and the text (p. 7) report t(1596) = 4.90, p_holm < 0.001; possibly a sign typo for 1.43.

Study 2 GPT-4 configuration DGR contrasts (p. 5) are printed with negative signs (Naive vs Base b = -0.04; Parameter-modified vs Base b = -0.18) although Table 2 slopes are higher for the modified conditions; the sign reflects Base minus configuration.
The supplement (Tables S1-S10, Figs. S1-S3: demographics, robustness with Sentence-BERT, preregistration deviations) is not in this PDF and was not checked.
Whether the human essays in Studies 1-3 overlap (all drawn from the same archive) is not stated.
notes: Candidate record title differs from the document title. The seed library labeled this paper 'RCT'; the PDF shows no assignment of people, only comparisons of human and GPT-4 essays, so all studies are ai_vs_human. Treatment arm is coded as the GPT-4 condition and control as human so that 'treatment_lower' means GPT-4 output is less diverse. Contrasts between GPT-4 configurations and between the two human groups are recorded with comparison_type 'other'. The paper also reports, in footnote 3 (p. 4) and Table S1, models with only log essays and authorship dummies; these are not listed separately.
